Chapter 4 turns from the ethics of action to its metaphysics. Kṛṣṇa reveals that the yoga he is teaching is an ancient one, lost and now restored, and explains his own recurring descents into the world: whenever dharma fades and its opposite rises, he takes birth, age after age, to protect the good and check the wicked. He then draws a distinction his listener will need for the rest of the poem — between the caste order he says he himself created by guṇa and karma, and its corruption into hereditary status. The chapter's center is the paradox of action-in-inaction: one who sees inaction within action and action within inaction is the truly wise, and the reader who understands this is no longer bound by what they do. Kṛṣṇa surveys the many kinds of sacrifice practised by different seekers — sacrifice of wealth, of austerity, of the breath itself — and ranks the sacrifice of knowledge above them all, since knowledge burns away the residue of past action as fire burns fuel. The chapter closes with Kṛṣṇa urging Arjuna to seek that knowledge from a teacher, to cut through doubt with it, and to stand up and act.
